I am a second-year PhD student in physics at Virginia Tech, working with ChunJun Cao.
My research sits around quantum information, quantum foundations, quantum gravity, quantum mereology, and quantum computing. I am especially interested in cases where the right quantum-information language turns a conceptual question into something that can be computed or tested.

title: Over Greenland
text:
Coming back from a month in Vienna, I flew over Iceland, Greenland, and the northeast coast of Canada, and I got to see some pretty cool things.
Anyway, here is what I saw, in order.
A biiiiig ice sheet, which I thought was a flat cloud at first.

Then, as land appears, you notice that it is, in fact, ice. The blue tint is because the windows were slowly losing their tint.

The next three images show cool new details appearing: rugged rock and an isolated rocky island in the middle of the ice.



Mountains with cool shadows.

A small piece of rock protruding from the ice. I wonder how big it is.

In a wider view, we can see water channels of different colors: icy blue (maybe there is ice in there) and deeper blue. The deeper blue ones appear disconnected from the ice???

The boundaries between huge ice sheets and the sea are very cool. It’s pretty much a glacier, but in the sea. Here are a few images of that.




The ice sheets extending inland in flowing shapes are neat because, if you look closely, the ice has a lot of surface structure. I think what we are seeing are marks from the downward flow of the ice. Interestingly, the curves we see on the ice are a lot smoother than the curves along the edges of the ice riverbed. Maybe that’s because it’s behaving somewhat like a fluid?



We see more of these marks in the next image, but we also see very clearly the two colors that water can take. Basically, the color of lakes versus the sea, I think. We also see more of the topography thanks to the shadows (not to be confused with the lakes).


A picture of a tiny melted area in the huge ice flow. No idea why it melted, but we can see a valley leading to it.

Leaving the ice behind a bit, we can start noticing cliffs in the distance! A massive slab wall for the brave. And zooming in, we also see a minuscule beach (I think).


So much water trapped in lakes.

The landscape looks a lot steeper in the distance.

I can now say that I have seen an iceberg.

Many icebergs.


This particular valley seems very cool. It looks deep, and somehow like it’s curving.


Now for some water things. Water coming from two distinct valleys/ice rivers is merging, and the two streams somehow have different colors. Why is there more mud in one of them??

Pictures of the coast. Very difficult to say what altitude these were taken from. 100 km or 5 km? Commercial flights are typically at 10 km, apparently. I think that difficulty in figuring out the distance is something fractals share!



Super far away. I feel like that distant ice flow is probably close to 100 km away from me. And look at all that ice flowing to the ocean!




And again, the farther I look, the taller the cliffs look. There is also a small mountain sticking out of the ice.

Tiny islands. But also, look at the color gradient in the water! Fresh water doing something weird to seawater? Minerals being ground down by the ice and washed down to the sea? It’s really surprising how visible it is.


Finishing up with a wide view and cool clouds.


Actually, finishing up with a circular double rainbow I saw just past Greenland. Zoom in; it’s not that small.


And some clouds with a super neat texture.

And a jet with a trail that somehow looks black.




Final thoughts: look out the window more, and save some money to go spend a month in Greenland. And why didn’t I see these things on the previous 10 flights? Turns out it makes sense: I need a window seat (2/9), a daytime flight (~1/2), good weather (???), and to not be busy watching a movie (~1/2). So, less than a 5% chance.

title: Research
text: I use tools from quantum information to study how structure, objectivity, and locality can emerge from quantum systems.

title: Research
text:
Objectivity and Quantum Error Correction
Quantum Darwinism asks how many observers can agree on stable, classical facts about a quantum system. My recent work studies this through operator algebra quantum error correction, where objectivity can be phrased as a local recoverability problem.

Algebraic conditions for objectivity
Connections between redundancy, classicality, and recoverable information
Stabilizer-code models and Clifford simulations

title: Research
text:
Quantum Mereology and Emergent Locality
Quantum mereology asks how the parts of a quantum system should be chosen. I am interested in when a choice of degrees of freedom makes a system look local, geometric, or field-like, even if that structure was not obvious from the original description.

Wave packets from spectra
Emergent lattice descriptions
Locality from choices of factorization or mode basis

title: Research
text:
Quantum Gravity and Information
I am broadly interested in how tools from quantum information and error correction can clarify gravitational questions, especially questions about emergence, observables, and the role of subsystems.
